proposal.title: Verifiable donation ledger for a student volunteer club, anchored on Bitcoin signet

proposal.problem: The volunteer club raises money for three to four campaigns every term, such as winter clothing drives and school book collections, and collects roughly 250 donations a term from students, alumni and local shops. Today the treasurer keeps the accounts in a shared spreadsheet and posts a summary on social media at the end of each campaign. Donors cannot check that their own donation was counted, and nobody outside the board can tell whether a row was edited or deleted after the summary was posted. At the last general assembly the board spent about 6 hours answering questions about where the money went, and two members asked for an external audit that the club cannot afford. When the treasurer changes every year, the spreadsheet history and the receipts are partly lost, so the new board cannot prove the previous term's totals either. Low trust keeps donations small: the club believes that a visible, checkable record would bring back donors who stopped giving after earlier doubts.
proposal.mission: Give the Club treasurer a simple way to record every donation and expense as linked data whose weekly fingerprint is anchored on the Bitcoin signet, so that each Donor can prove their own donation is in the ledger and a Club auditor can verify the whole term's accounts without trusting the spreadsheet or the board.
proposal.outcome: A donor opens the receipt link on their phone and sees that their donation is included in an anchored weekly batch; the auditor runs one check over the term and sees every batch match its anchor, and any edited or deleted entry fails the check at once.

proposal.techWhy: schema.org gives ready terms for donations, money amounts and campaigns, and PROV-O records who entered or corrected each record and when, so the ledger is standard linked data that outlives one treasurer. Records are serialised as JSON-LD for the web pages and handled in Python with RDFLib. SHACL shapes, run with pySHACL, refuse a record without an amount, a campaign or a receipt before it can enter a batch. Oxigraph stores the records and answers SPARQL queries for campaign totals. Stable IRIs give every record a permanent receipt link, and the KVKK regime decides that names never leave the club's store.

goals.goal: Donors and auditors can check the ledger without asking the board

goals.goal: Every donation and expense is a valid linked-data record
goals.why: an invalid or missing record makes the proof meaningless

goals.goal: Every weekly batch is anchored on signet
goals.why: an unanchored batch can still be changed silently

goals.goal: No personal data reaches the blockchain
goals.why: KVKK and the club's donors forbid it

proposal.spec: The system lets the club treasurer enter each donation and expense as a JSON-LD record using schema.org and PROV-O terms, validates it against SHACL shapes and stores it in Oxigraph with a stable IRI. Every week it closes a batch, computes the SHA-256 hash of each canonical record, builds a Merkle tree as Bitcoin does for transactions, and anchors the Merkle root in an OP_RETURN output of a signet transaction through a Bitcoin Core node. A donor's receipt link shows the record, its Merkle path and the anchoring transaction and recomputes the root. The auditor page checks every batch of a term against its anchor. The system refuses invalid records, never edits an anchored record, and never writes personal data to the chain.

scenarios.text: Given a donation recorded in a batch that has been anchored, when the donor opens their receipt link, then the page recomputes the Merkle root from the inclusion proof and shows that it matches the signet anchor

Given an expense whose amount was edited in the store after its batch was anchored, when the auditor runs the term check, then that batch is reported as not matching its anchor and the changed record is named
Given a week with an odd number of records, when the batch is closed, then the last hash is duplicated at each odd level as Bitcoin does, and every record's inclusion proof still verifies

proposal.useCase: Club treasurer: enter donation, enter expense, close week. Donor: open receipt link, verify inclusion. Club auditor: run term check, download report.

proposal.activity: The treasurer enters a donation or an expense in the form. The record is checked against the shapes; if it is invalid it is refused with the reasons. Otherwise it is stored with a stable IRI in the open batch of the week. At the end of the week the treasurer closes the batch: the records are hashed, the Merkle tree is built and the root is sent to the anchoring service, which broadcasts a signet transaction and waits for one confirmation. The transaction id is stored with the batch and every donor's receipt link becomes verifiable.
proposal.sequence: The treasurer's page posts the record to the ledger service. The service asks pySHACL to validate it, writes it to Oxigraph and answers with its IRI. On closing a batch the service queries the week's records with SPARQL, canonicalises each one, hashes it with SHA-256, builds the Merkle tree and calls the Bitcoin Core signet node over RPC to create, fund and broadcast a transaction with an OP_RETURN output holding the root. The receipt page asks the service for a record and its Merkle path, recomputes the root and asks the node for the transaction to compare them.

proposal.classModel: Donation is a schema:DonateAction with a schema:MonetaryAmount, a campaign, a date and a salted donor pseudonym; Expense has an amount, a purpose, a campaign and a receipt file. Both are prov:Entity, generated by an EntryActivity associated with the Treasurer agent. LedgerBatch groups the records of one week and holds the Merkle root; Anchor has a txid, a block height and the root; InclusionProof links one record to its batch through a list of sibling hashes. A record belongs to exactly one batch; a correction is a new record derived from the old one with prov:wasRevisionOf.

proposal.model_Data: Design-level class diagram: Donation and Expense (prov:Entity, schema.org typed) generated by EntryActivity associated with the Treasurer agent; LedgerBatch holds a Merkle root; Anchor holds txid, block height and root; shapes DonationShape, ExpenseShape and BatchShape guard them.
proposal.model_Security: State machine of a batch: open, closed, anchoring, anchored; records can be added only while open, a closed batch is hashed once, and an anchored batch is never edited - a correction enters the next batch as a revision of the old record.
proposal.model_User_interface: Receipt page: one green or red result with amount, campaign, date and a link to the signet transaction; readable on a phone, no login. Treasurer form shows each shape violation next to its field.
proposal.model_Interaction: Sequence: donor scans the QR code on the paper receipt or taps the link in the thank-you message; the page loads the record and its proof, recomputes the root, fetches the anchor and shows the result.
proposal.model_Architecture: Deployment view: one Python ledger service with Oxigraph embedded, one Bitcoin Core signet node reached over RPC, and static web pages; the node address and wallet are configuration, so the club can move the service to another machine.
proposal.model_Interface: Component diagram: TreasurerForm and AuditorPage call the LedgerAPI; LedgerAPI uses Store (Oxigraph, SPARQL) and AnchorService (Bitcoin Core RPC); ReceiptPage calls a read-only VerifyAPI that returns a record, its Merkle path and its txid.
proposal.chainDesign: Bitcoin signet with a Bitcoin Core node: each week's records are hashed with SHA-256 and combined in a Merkle tree built the way Bitcoin builds a block's transaction tree, and the 32-byte root is written in one OP_RETURN output of a signet transaction. Donors verify inclusion with a Merkle path, as SPV clients do. A blockchain is needed because the club's own database or spreadsheet can be changed by whoever controls it; an anchor in a public, proof-of-work-secured chain lets anyone outside the board check that past records were not altered, without trusting the board or paying an auditor.
